newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico to announce petrochemical sale plans soon.
newsitem.headline: Mexico to announce petrochemical sale plans soon.

text.p: The Mexican government plans in the next few days to announce a new initiative on the troubled and much-delayed privatisation of Mexico's petrochemical plants, a legislator and an official source said.
Francisco Curi, head of the energy commission in the Chamber of Deputies, said President Ernesto Zedillo would announce shortly the government's strategy on petrochemicals.
An official source, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the plan would unveil "a framework for private investment in current and future petrochemical plants".
He would not be drawn on whether the state would retain majority control but hinted that at least a partial stake in existing secondary petrochemical plants would be privatised.

Zedillo's government announced plans 18 months ago to sell off secondary petrochemical plants but stiff opposition from within his Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), union criticism and legal problems have prevented any action.
Local news media have speculated that the government may now stop short of selling majority stakes in existing plants.
The government said last October that 10 plants would be spun off by the end of 1996 but the first sale, planned for April, has yet to happen.

Public ownership of Mexico's oil industry is considered sacred by many in Mexico since oil was expropriated from foreign companies by the government in 1938 and turned into a symbol of Mexican sovereignty.

The PRI itself voted at a party assembly last month to oppose the privatisation of the petrochemical industry -- and Curi said he hoped Zedillo's announcement next week would take the PRI's opinion into account.
The powerful oil workers union, meanwhile, were reported by news media as saying it would agree to a privatisation as long as the union could hold a stake in the privatised plants.
